items.name: Cuberdon
items.summary: A cone-shaped sugar candy with a hard outer shell and soft, syrupy interior, flavoured with raspberry. Invented in Ghent around 1873 by a pharmacist named Romain Lafait. Known locally as 'neuzekes' (little noses). The authentic Ghent cuberdon is protected by a regional quality label.

items.name: Liège Waffle
items.summary: A rich, dense waffle made with brioche-style dough and pearl sugar that caramelises during baking, creating a crisp, sweet crust. Created in the 18th century by the chef of the Prince-Bishop of Liège. Denser and sweeter than the Brussels waffle, it is eaten plain as a street food.

items.name: Brussels Waffle
items.summary: A light, rectangular waffle with deep pockets, crisp exterior and airy interior, made from a yeast-leavened batter. Introduced at the 1964 World's Fair in New York by Maurice Vermersch. Traditionally served warm with whipped cream, strawberries, or chocolate. Lighter and larger than the Liège waffle.

items.name: Belgian Waffle
items.summary: The umbrella term for Belgian-style waffles sold internationally, typically modelled on the Brussels waffle. The term became widespread after the 1962 and 1964 World's Fairs. In Belgium itself, locals distinguish between the Liège and Brussels varieties rather than using the generic term.

items.name: Speculoos
items.summary: A spiced shortcrust biscuit traditionally baked for the feast of Saint Nicholas (6 December). Made with a blend of cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, ginger, cardamom and white pepper. The Belgian version (speculoos) is thinner and crispier than the Dutch speculaas. Lotus Bakeries' Lotus Biscoff made speculoos a global pantry staple.

items.name: Mattentaart
items.summary: A small pastry from the city of Geraardsbergen, filled with a curd cheese (matte) and egg mixture, enclosed in a puff pastry shell. The recipe dates to the 13th century and the Mattentaart of Geraardsbergen holds a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) from the European Union since 2007.

items.name: Rijsttaart
items.summary: A Belgian rice tart made from short-crust pastry filled with a creamy rice pudding, baked until the top is lightly set. A staple of Belgian bakeries, it is simpler and less sweet than French pastry equivalents. Often eaten cold, sliced into squares. Regional variations exist across Flanders and Wallonia.

items.name: Tarte au Riz
items.summary: The Walloon cousin of the Flemish rijsttaart. A shortcrust pastry tart filled with sweetened rice pudding, with a slightly more custardy texture than the Flemish version. Originating in Verviers and the Liège region, it is a protected regional speciality. Often topped with a thin caramel glaze.

items.name: Merveilleux
items.summary: A delicate meringue dessert sandwiched with whipped cream and coated in chocolate shavings, crumbled meringue or praline. Originally from the Lille–Brussels border region in the 18th century, the merveilleux was revived and popularised by Brussels pâtissier Frédéric Vaucamp from the 1990s onwards. Now an icon of Belgian-French border patisserie.
